Assessment of Clients with Cardiovascular Disorders

headings.title: Introduction to Cardiovascular Assessment
headings.content: Cardiovascular assessment forms the bedrock of detecting heart and vascular pathologies early. A systematic evaluation prevents catastrophic complications like acute myocardial infarction or hypertensive crises, which frequently burden emergency wards across Nigerian tertiary hospitals. Nurses must approach this process with a blend of keen observation and methodical technique. The core objective is determining how efficiently the heart pumps blood to meet the metabolic demands of peripheral tissues. Mastery of this skill enables rapid identification of hemodynamic instability before overt clinical deterioration occurs.

headings.title: Gathering the Health History
headings.content:
A detailed health history uncovers critical risk factors that physical exams alone might miss. When interviewing a client, prioritize unravelling the chief complaint, particularly the exact character, radiation, and precipitating factors of chest pain. Inquire deeply into past medical history, family history of premature cardiovascular disease, and lifestyle habits like smoking or heavy alcohol consumption. 

- **Chest Pain**: Investigate onset, location, duration, and aggravating factors using standard clinical mnemonics.
- **Dyspnea**: Differentiate between exertional breathlessness, orthopnea, and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea.
- **Edema**: Note timing and progression of swelling in the lower extremities.
- **Fatigue**: Assess for unusual tiredness that limits daily activities.

headings.title: Inspection and Palpation Techniques
headings.content:
Physical examination begins at the bedside with careful observation of the client's general appearance, skin color, and respiratory effort. Cyanosis or pallor signals poor tissue oxygenation. Palpation focuses on locating the point of maximal impulse and feeling for thrills.

| Landmark | Exact Location | Clinical Significance |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Aortic Area** | Second right intercostal space at the sternal border | Evaluates aortic valve sounds and murmurs |
| **Pulmonic Area** | Second left intercostal space at the sternal border | Evaluates pulmonic valve abnormalities |
| **Tricuspid Area** | Fourth or fifth left intercostal space at the sternal border | Assesses tricuspid valve function |
| **Mitral Area** | Fifth left intercostal space at the midclavicular line | Locates the apical pulse or point of maximal impulse |

headings.title: Auscultation of Heart Sounds
headings.content:
Listening to the heart requires a quiet environment and a stethoscope equipped with both a bell and a diaphragm. The diaphragm effectively transmits high-pitched sounds like S1 and S2, while the bell detects low-pitched murmurs and gallops like S3 or S4. 

S1 represents the closure of the mitral and tricuspid valves, marking the beginning of systole and sounding loudest at the apex. S2 marks the closure of the aortic and pulmonic valves, signaling the end of systole and sounding loudest at the base. Listening closely for extra sounds or abnormal timing helps nurses identify potential heart failure or valve dysfunction early.

headings.title: Diagnostic Evaluation and Monitoring
headings.content: Physical assessment alone rarely provides a complete picture, requiring supportive diagnostic tests. The 12-lead electrocardiogram remains the gold standard for evaluating electrical activity and identifying ischemic changes or arrhythmias. Blood investigations such as cardiac biomarkers—specifically troponin levels—help confirm myocardial necrosis. In many Nigerian clinical environments, nurses must also coordinate basic imaging studies like chest radiographs to assess cardiac silhouette enlargement and pulmonary congestion.

headings.title: Documentation and Reporting in Nigerian Practice
headings.content: Accurate, timely documentation closes the loop in patient care. In busy Nigerian wards, where nurse-to-client ratios can be challenging, clear charting prevents miscommunication during shift handovers. Document all objective findings, vital sign trends, and reported symptoms using standard hospital formats. Never delay reporting critical abnormalities like sudden drop in blood pressure or severe chest pain to the attending physician. Maintaining legible and comprehensive records also protects professional integrity and ensures continuity of safe nursing care.
